rv.q: Both actors, neither one immune to the lure of excess showmanship, are terrific -- stylish, disciplined, strikingly different -- in Sean Mathias' repertory stagings of Beckett's familiar 1953 masterwork, "Waiting for Godot," and Pinter's more rare, chilling and opaque "No Man's Land."

But it's the sense of rueful, wounded humanity that distinguishes them in plays that both hinge on co-dependent relationships, whether chilled by the icy breath of menace in Pinter's 1975 drama, or cloaked in the more clownish despair of Beckett's 1953 classic.
McKellen is a wonder. Stewart is marvelous.
But as directed by Sean Mathias, with sturdy supporting performances by Billy Crudup and Shuler Hensley, these productions find the pure entertainment value in existential emptiness.
The production succeeds because it lets Pinter's language do most of the work, and because McKellen and Stewart are such accomplished speakers of it.
If you have to pick one, 'No Man's Land' is the way to go.
It's a good thing, because it would be impossible to put across plays as head-scratchingly abstract as Godot and No Man's Land without tapping into their pathos as well as their verbal slapstick.
McKellen, exquisite in his poised buffoonery
Stewart and McKellen traverse the full range of humanity on stage, with moments of hope, fear and despair.

Although not as dramatically potent as Pinter's similarly plotted "The Caretaker," the play, like "Godot," gives two commanding performers an opportunity to provide a master class in acting. They're a treat.
But amid Pinter's elliptical storytelling and pregnant pauses and Beckett's existential mystery, ideas about power, class, memory and mortality get your gray matter buzzing.
They turn in solidly professional performances, efficiently directed by Sean Mathias, but pale in comparison to their illustrious costars.

While it was a marvelous idea to pair up Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen as the quintessential tramps Vladimir and Estragon in "Waiting for Godot," this revival of Beckett's existentialist classic is weighed down by Sean Mathias' problematic direction and the decision to perform it in repertory with Harold Pinter's 1975 drama "No Man's Land."
None of these productions has represented the performers at their peak.
McKellen and Stewart, legends of stage and screen, bring their considerable talents to bear on Pinter's cryptic masterpiece, creating an evening of theatrical magic.
